title: How to kickstart a marketplace: constrain by geography or category first, from 17 marketplaces
summary: Lenny shares research from interviews with founders and early employees at 17 major marketplaces. The first step to cracking the chicken-and-egg problem is to constrain the marketplace by geography or category, since the best way to get big is to start small. He also warns against over-relying on any single company's story.

principles.text: A marketplace connects demand and supply and leads to a financial transaction, without owning supply itself.
principles.quote: A marketplace business is one that **(1) connects demand** (i.e. people who want a thing) with **(2) supply** (i.e. people who have that thing), and **(3) leads to a financial transaction**.

principles.text: Starting a marketplace is hard because one side must commit before the other exists (chicken-and-egg).
principles.quote: it’s challenging to get the flywheel going. You must convince one side of the marketplace to commit before the other side.

principles.text: Constrain your initial marketplace; going small first is the fastest way to get big.
principles.quote: every single marketplace that I interviewed constrained their initial marketplace** to more quickly get to critical mass.

principles.text: Constrain by geography when supply and demand must meet physically; otherwise constrain by category.
principles.quote: If the offering requires supply and demand to be in the same physical location, the constraint is always geographical (e.g. a limited set of markets). Otherwise, it’s category-based (e.g. handmade goods).

principles.text: Don't over-index on one company's story; focus on the ways of thinking behind tactics, since past tactics often stop working.
principles.quote: focus more on ways of thinking and the cleverness behind the ideas –– not only the specific tactics. Many of the most successful growth levers of the past no longer work, or are significantly less effective.

principles.text: Many marketplaces succeeded primarily through product/market fit; growth levers accelerated and controlled growth rather than creating it.
principles.quote: For many of these companies, the primary reason they became successful was not because of some amazing growth insights – it was primarily because of great product/market fit
